turns.presentation_text: Poison Ivy didn't rise to the whoop in Harley's voice, and she didn't shift out from under Harley's chin. Even the tray don't wanna watch. So whatever you're sellin', it just lost its only buyer with a set of keys." "You wanna talk partnerships? I heard ya. 'We.' Real cute. One slow tap, no louder than the second chime. "Here's your accounting, and it's the last line I read out. turns.player_stimulus: Magpie shuffles in the transfer line, eyes on the corridor cameras. "Mess hall's done. What's next—punishment or opportunity?"

An' I ain't askin' twice."

Sit on my bench — I put the tray down. Or stand in that doorway an' watch that nice man write your name, an' I drop this whole thing right here on the floor an' clap for you while they walk ya out. Clock stopped, birdie. Mine's the one still tickin', an' right now I'm standin' in the aisle where the room can see exactly which one a' us is holdin' it." Then she walked the tray back to the table, set it down dead center between the two painted sides, and dropped onto the bench hip to hip with Ivy — arm slung back around her waist, other hand flat on the tabletop inside the chalk line, both hands where the whole row could count them. She leaned her head onto Ivy's shoulder, grinning out across the mess hall, all teeth, and stayed exactly where she was.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie asks the guard, "Did the nurse who reported you get reassigned—or disappeared?"
turns.presentation_text: Ivy didn't take back the arm Harley had slung around her waist, and she didn't turn her head toward the aisle. Her free hand crossed the wet ring, lifted Harley's palm off the tabletop where it sat inside the chalk line, and set it down flat on Harley's own knee — returning it to the side of the border Harley had drawn — before she laid her own hand open on the neutral wood between the two claims, fingers loose, palm up, where the whole row could count it. "Churches take collections, sweetheart. That's the whole difference. A greenhouse doesn't pass a plate — it decides what's worth watering. So here's the accounting, birdie, and it's short: the shine on that man's wrist was never the thing you were carrying. It was the tell. The same tell that had half this room pricing your pockets before you'd finished your first tray. Nobody at this table is going to reach into them — I told you that already, and I don't repeat myself for free. I only ever wanted to know which one you'd rather spend. The thing, or the room's attention. One of those grows back." Then she folded the open hand slowly on the wet ring — not a fist, just fingers curling shut over nothing — and left it closed on the neutral wood, tipping her chin once toward the dead-center tray while her eyes stayed on the guarded margin and never touched Harley. "And you. You called it a church in front of witnesses. Fine. Keep the joke — I'll keep the bench. You're sitting on it because I left it open, and the row watched me leave it open after the second chime and after you threw the count, which is the part that follows you out of this room. So put the tray down, put your hand back inside your own chalk, and let the men with the keys finish deciding there's nothing here worth writing up. Plant sale's over, Harley. You sat down. That was the answer." Down the margin, the guard Magpie had spoken to shifted his stance but kept his eyes fixed on the line; the question hung unanswered while the inmates at the nearby tables went quiet to watch the neutral wood under the hard fluorescents.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie fingers the token. "This buys a door. Question is whose door you want opened."

She spread her fingers against the denim, pressed once, and dragged them off slowly enough that the whole row could watch her read the thing she'd been handed. Then she slapped the wet ring with the same hand, hard, and left it there inside her own chalk line. "Plant sale's over. You sat down. That was the answer. Aw, sweetheart — listen to you. Whole mess hall fulla paste an' you just gave yourself the last word. Real tidy. Real quiet. Hey! Birdie! You still in that doorway? 'Cause Red just closed the market an' kept the bench, an' I'm the one sittin' on it." Above the next table, the fluorescent tube flickered, popped, and rained a brief shower of glass dust onto the trays below, and a ripple of flinches ran down the row. She hooked her boot up onto the bench rail and rocked back, one arm still slung around Ivy's waist, the other flat on the table. She leaned her weight into Ivy's shoulder — not a shove, a stacking — and rolled her eyes across the guarded margin where the boots had settled, then dragged them back down the hall to the doorway end. Two chimes down, one tray in the middle, an' not one person at this table has said a word worth the paperwork yet." She turned her face into Ivy's shoulder, mouth against the collar of the jumpsuit, voice pitched down under the scrape of benches and boots — private, but her shoulders stayed open to the room so the whole row could see her doing it. Her hand on the tabletop flexed once, knuckles whitening on the wet ring, then went loose again. "You got your headline, Red. I got the bench. Wanna see what I do when the light goes out? 'Cause I don't do sermons, sweetheart. I do receipts." She reached across with two fingers, hooked the dead-center tray's rim, and drew it an inch off the table — tilting it so the paste slop slid to the lip and hung there — then swung it out toward the doorway end of the mess hall, chin up, grin wide and all teeth, both hands where the whole row could count them. "Birdie! Birdie, lookit me! Ivy gave ya the quiet version an' the room didn't blink. So here's the loud one, an' it's the last time I'm gonna say it with both feet on the floor: you show me the pocket, you sit on this bench, or you stand there an' let the nice man with the watch write your name while I drop this whole tray an' clap. Clock's mine. Bench is mine. Sermon's over. Pick a lane, an' pick it 'fore the lights gutter again."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie nods at the scratched key tag. "East stairwell. That's where trouble lives."
turns.presentation_text: Ivy didn't turn her head when the east stairwell door banged somewhere past the mess hall wall, and she didn't lift her hip off the neutral wood at the bench's center. A guard's radio crackled down the margin; she let it roll unanswered, then reached across with two fingers and laid them on the dead-center tray's rim — not pulling it, not tilting it, just holding it flat where neither side of Harley's chalk line owned it — while the closed hand she'd left on the wood opened slowly beside it, palm up, empty, where the row could keep counting it. "Hear that. The building answered for you, birdie — east door on the hinge, radio on the wall. That's two more voices in this room than the woman standing in the doorway has used. Harley's clock ran out and mine doesn't tick, so I'll say this once and keep it short, because the room is done being patient with either of us. The offer hasn't moved an inch. Sit where I can count your hands, or don't. But the lights are guttering, the men with the keys have finished deciding, and nothing at this table is waiting on a countdown anymore — only on what you do with your feet. I don't chase. I cultivate. And I've already told you which of those two ends with you still standing upright in this room." She left her fingers on the rim a beat longer, then drew them back and turned her wrist over a final time on the wet ring the plastic had been tracing — palm up, fingers loose, the same flat display she'd held since before the first chime — and let it rest on the neutral wood without tapping the bench beside her hip or reaching for Harley's hand inside the chalk line. Her eyes stayed level across the mess hall on the guarded margin where the boots had settled, shoulder still under Harley's arm, hip still centered, and she gave back not one inch of the wood while the fluorescents hummed their next stutter overhead.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie doesn't soften her voice. "If you sell me out, I'll make sure you regret it before lights-out."
turns.presentation_text: The plastic bench rail scraped as Harley came off it, and she brought her palm down flat over the back of Ivy's hand where it lay on the dead-center tray's rim — not prying, just stacking hers on top, two fingers becoming two of them in plain view of the whole row. "Greenhouse. Seedbed. Fixture. Sweets, that's three sermons in one breath an' you didn't once look at me while you read 'em. Tray's the only thing in this room you keep your eyes on — tray an' the wall." She hooked two fingers under Ivy's chin — light and unhurried, the same way Ivy turned her wrist on the table — and turned Ivy's face off the guarded margin and back onto hers, holding it one beat before letting go and swinging her own chin out across the mess hall toward the doorway end. "Hey! Birdie! Yeah, you — standin' in that doorway like wet laundry. Red closed the market. I never closed mine. Mine's still open, an' you're still the only customer at the counter, an' the man with the watch is walkin' this way right now to see who's buyin'. So which is it, huh? Pocket, bench, or his little book?" Under the hard overheads the long room went quiet along its length. Harley planted one boot up on the bench beside the tray and rocked her weight onto it, tipping her head toward the guarded margin without turning her shoulders from the room, both hands out where the row could count them — one laid over Ivy's on the tray, one open and empty in the air. "So here's the last thing I say with my feet on the floor, an' I ain't sayin' it twice nice: show the pocket, sit the bench, or stand there an' let him write your name while I clap. Clock's mine, birdie. Red can keep the bench — I'll take the noise." At the margin a guard tapped his radio once and took a single step toward the contested table, hand resting on his belt. Harley dropped off the bench rail and landed hip to hip with Ivy, slinging her arm back around Ivy's waist, chin up, grin wide and all teeth, both hands still exactly where the row could count them — and stayed there.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie lets the guards hurry her along. "This isn't over. It's just moving rooms."
turns.presentation_text: The mess hall door clanged shut behind Magpie and the echo rolled down the long tables, thinning against stacked empty trays until the room's hard lighting had nothing left to bounce off but quiet. Ivy didn't turn her head toward it. Her free hand came across and lifted Harley's palm off the back of her own knuckles — not prying, just rolling her wrist beneath until Harley's fingers rested loose in her open hand — and she laid the pair flat on the neutral wood between the chalk line and her own side of the bench, both palms up where the row could count them. "That's the hinge answering. Not her. It'll have to do. I don't chase, sweetheart — I've said it twice now, and the third time I start charging for the repetition." Then two fingers hooked under Harley's chin in answer, light and unhurried, the same pressure Harley had used on her, turning Harley's face off the doorway and back onto hers and holding it one beat — long enough for the nearest table to catch it — before she let go and set her hand back down open on the wood. "And you. Two fingers under my chin in front of the whole ward, a tray held over an aisle like a headline, my name used as your volume. That's a receipt, and I keep those. Don't ever mistake the bench I left open for a stage I handed you. You sat down because I let it stand empty after the second chime — that's the version the room takes out of here, and the only one I'll cosign." She settled her hip back into the exact center of the bench, shoulder still under Harley's arm, and let her eyes travel the guarded margin once — boots, watch, pen, the plastic chairs ranked along the wall — before bringing them back to the neutral wood and the open hand she'd left there. "So here's the last line, read at the volume the room has left us. The tray sits in the middle because neither of us owns it. Nobody's name is on that pad, and it's going to stay that way, because this corner has already said everything worth writing down. The count was never mine to keep and never hers to take — it just stopped. Plant sale's closed. Whatever was in the doorway is the door's problem now. The greenhouse is still open, and I decide what grows in it."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie keeps her eyes on the guard's gold watch while she pushes food around her tray. "Pretty things never stay pretty in here for long."
turns.presentation_text: Harley swung her legs over the bench and stood, bringing both palms down on the tabletop so the trays jumped and clattered. Her eyes tracked Magpie's drift toward the guard, and her grin widened when the hard mess-hall light caught the gold watch on the guard's wrist. "Well, well—Mags got a magpie jones already? Gold watch, huh? That's a real pretty way to get your teeth rearranged." She kept her voice pitched across the long tables. "Hey! Sparkly! You gonna stand there makin' love to a wristwatch, or you gonna give the class a show?" A tray clattered at the next table, and a guard's radio crackled from the room's margin, pulling a few quick glances. Harley snatched a plastic spoon off her tray and flicked it spinning across the floor in Magpie's general direction. "Ivy, lookit this. New girl's already shoppin'. Ain't that adorable?"

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie murmurs to Ivy, "Whatever happened to that nurse who kept staring at our table last month?"
turns.presentation_text: Ivy didn't stand. She set two fingers on the edge of the jumped tray and steadied it, her eyes sliding from Harley's flung spoon across the hard-lit mess hall to the flash of gold on the guard's wrist at the room's margin, then over to Magpie's drift. Long tables and plastic chairs kept every sightline exposed beneath the worn murals. "Sit down, Harley. You've already rung the bell for the whole room. Let's see whether the new girl can walk herself back from the edge without you pushing her over it." Ivy tilted her head toward Magpie, her voice pitched low enough to carry only across the table line, one hand turning a wilted lettuce leaf over like a specimen. "You heard something pretty, didn't you. That's the trouble with shiny things in here—every guard in the room is watching to see who covets what. You've got about four seconds to decide if you want to be a rumor or a lesson. Pick fast."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie flicks a glance at Harley. "You want a distraction. She wants a favor. I'm listening to both of you."
turns.presentation_text: Harley didn't sit. She stayed half-risen at the bench edge and crowed down the table line, "Sit down? Sit DOWN? Ivie, baby, the bell's already rung—might as well charge admission. Look at 'er, she's still floatin' at that wrist like it's got a heartbeat." Then she swung one leg over the bench and sidled two steps into the open lane between the tables, chin up, both hands loose at her sides, her grin still angled at the gold flash on the guard's wrist and at Magpie's drift. The lane smelled of bleach and reheated gravy; hard overhead panels laid a flat shine along the plastic chairbacks and left the worn murals dim. "Hey, Sparkly! Four seconds is a long time in here, and you're burnin' it starin' at somebody else's jewelry. So what's it gonna be, huh—you gonna snatch it and give us all a real show, or you gonna crawl back to the bench and let me tell everybody you chickened out?" She hooked the flung spoon back toward herself with the side of her shoe, scooped it up, and tapped it twice against her palm like a little baton, eyes still tracking the guard's wrist and Magpie's approach line. "C'mon, I'll even be your coach. One twitch, Mags. One itsy-bitsy twitch and this whole room gets real interesting."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie notes the scratched tag on the guard's key ring without staring. "East stairwell must be popular."
turns.presentation_text: The mess hall held its hard white light over the worn murals, and the murmur rolling off the long tables had turned toward the lane between them. Ivy laid the wilted lettuce leaf down flat on the tray, stem-first, and rose without hurry — no slap of palm, no scrape of bench on the scuffed floor. She stepped into the lane Harley had opened and stopped half a pace behind her shoulder, near enough that her voice would land in Harley's ear and nowhere else, one hand resting light on the table's edge. "Harley. That's twice now. You've made the room look at you, which is what you want, and you've made it look at the new girl, which is what she doesn't. Put the spoon down. You can have the audience back after I've finished with her." Then she turned her head across the cafeteria — past the flash of gold at the guard's wrist, to the line Magpie was drifting along — and exhaled slowly, the kind of exhale that carried nothing visible and everything deliberate, her eyes tracking from the watch back to Magpie and staying there while two fingers straightened the collar of her uniform. "Sparkly. Come here. Not to the wrist, to me. You're standing in a lane between a guard who's already counting steps and a woman who thinks your appetite is a party favor—that's two kinds of trouble and neither one is yours yet. Sit at our table, eat something that isn't metal, and tell me what you thought you saw. If it's worth anything, you keep your teeth and I keep my patience. If it's not, you'll be a rumor by lights-out. Decide." Ivy sat back down on the bench, spine straight, palms flat on either side of her tray — settled, occupied, unbothered. She did not look at the second guard shifting off the wall behind her; she watched the empty stretch of floor between the tables, where Magpie would either stop or wouldn't. The room was hers to steer, and the new arrival's appetite was a lever just handed to her.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie whispers, "If I help you move that packet, you don't sell me to Harley when it goes wrong."
turns.presentation_text: Under the hard lights, the room's noise kept running—trays clattering, plastic chairs scraping the scuffed floor, the worn murals staring down. Ivy didn't rise. She stayed seated exactly where she was, hooked the empty second tray with two fingers, and dragged it across the long table to the space beside her, clearing a place with the unhurried economy of someone staking out a planting row. She said, "Harley. Your four seconds are spent, and you're still standing in the middle of the room holding a spoon like it's a microphone. Sit down. The audience isn't going anywhere—you'll still be funny in an hour. The new girl might not be." She rolled a single grain of rice between thumb and forefinger until it cracked, letting the powder sift down onto the tray, and kept her eyes on the open stretch of floor between the tables. Her voice stayed at the same low, level register—no strain, no hurry, nothing the guards could point to as a threat. Then, without lifting it, she said, "Sparkly. What I'm offering you is a graft, not a gift. You sit here, you eat something that isn't metal, you tell me one true thing—and this room lets you keep your name. You don't, and you keep the lane, the guard, and whatever the walls feel like doing to you before lights-out. I don't need your appetite. I need to know if you're something that can be cultivated, or something bright and disposable that wandered in front of the wrong window. Say it out loud, so we all hear the same answer."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie smiles without warmth. "What would you trade for a guard looking the wrong way for ten seconds?"
turns.presentation_text: Harley didn't move toward the table. She turned a half-step so the open lane lay at her back, spun the plastic spoon once over her knuckles, and let it clatter flat on the edge of Ivy's dragged-out tray—resting there, not sitting. "A graft? A GRAFT? Ivie, sweetheart, you hear yourself? You sound like a lady sellin' ferns at a farmers' market. Meanwhile I'm over here runnin' a carnival." She hooked a thumb toward the flash of gold at the guard's wrist, then spread both arms wide at the room, chin high, grin all teeth. "Hey, everybody! Quick show of hands—who wants the shiny thing and who wants to hear a lecture about mulch? I know, I know, tough call. Sparkly, you're killin' me, you're still standin' in that lane like somebody's holdin' a magnet under your chin. Ivy's offerin' you a seat and a salad. I'm offerin' you somethin' better. Front row. Free. All you gotta do is pick." She planted both hands on her hips, rocked back on her heels, and tipped her head toward Magpie's line across the scuffed floor without dropping the grin. "C'mon. One true thing, she says. I'll settle for one fun thing. Say somethin' that isn't 'yes, ma'am' and the whole ward buys you a drink—metaphorically, we're in Arkham, the drinks are tap water and regret. Or keep starin' at that wrist and let the nice guard decide what happens next. Your four seconds were up two minutes ago, pumpkin. Clock's still tickin'." At the far end of the mess hall, a trustee stopped wiping the counter, rag motionless, eyes fixed on the lane.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie palms the mess hall token under the tray. "Little things buy bigger mistakes in Arkham."
turns.presentation_text: Ivy did not rise. She set one finger against the bowl of the spoon Harley had left on the tray's rim, tipped it flat, and slid it off the edge to rest beside her own fork, handling the prop without looking up at the woman who had thrown it. The mess hall's hard fluorescence flickered over the long tables, and the room's parallel attention stayed pinned on the open lane as Ivy spoke across it, voice level. "Harley. You've had your show. The room laughed, the guard counted steps, and the new girl is still standing in the lane. That doesn't make this a carnival—it makes it a tab, and I don't pay other people's tabs. You want the audience, you've got it. But the next line out of this table is mine, and you'll sit for it or you'll be scenery." She pressed the heel of her thumb into the wilted lettuce leaf, flattening it stem-first against the tray. Under the fluorescent flicker, a single pale tendril uncurled from the split vein and reached half a centimeter toward her knuckle before she closed her hand and stilled it. Her eyes lifted at last from the tray and tracked down the open lane—past Harley's planted stance and spread arms, past the flash of gold at the guard's wrist, to the far door and the trustee who had stopped moving beside the tray return. The far door's magnetic lock clicked once, then held. Ivy registered that click, then held her gaze on the stretch of floor where Magpie's drift had stalled. "Sparkly. That click was the far door. The trustee by the trays just forgot how to walk. You have one sentence of runway left before this room resets and every offer on this table expires with it. So here's mine, said once: sit down, eat something that isn't metal, and tell me what you actually came for. Not the watch. Not the shine. The thing underneath. Do that, and the lane forgets you were ever in it. Don't, and you can explain your appetite to whoever opens that door."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie kicks a ceramic shard aside. "Someone's going to blame us for this mess unless we move."
turns.presentation_text: Harley laughed — a real one, loud and sharp, head thrown back so the whole mess hall heard it ring off the worn murals and the hard overhead lights. She let it die off slowly, then reached over and scooped the plastic spoon up off the rim of Ivy's tray with two fingers, not hiding the theft at all, holding it up between them like a trophy. "Scenery? Scenery?! Ivie, sweetheart, I've been scenery and I've been the whole damn show, and lemme tell ya, scenery don't get free snacks. You hear that click? Half the room heard that click. You know who's still standin' in the middle of the floor with the lights on her? That's right, baby. Not the mulch. Me." Then she turned her back on Ivy deliberately — slow, showy, the kind of turn that said she knew exactly what it cost — and pointed the spoon down the lane at the stalled stretch of floor where Magpie's drift had stopped, then swung the point toward the far door and the frozen trustee beside the tray return. "Sparkly! You're still here? After all that? Attagirl, you got more spine than the salad bar. But listen, he's right about one thing — one sentence. So here's yours: door's about to open, watch is about to walk out on its own two legs, and I'm the only one in this room who ain't gonna make you sign a permission slip to breathe. So which way you gonna dance, pumpkin? Toward the shine, or toward the baton?" She planted the spoon between her teeth like a rose stem, stepped two more paces into the open lane so the far door sat at her back and the lane split behind her, and widened her stance — hips cocked, chin up, both hands free, grinning around the plastic like it was the funniest thing that had ever happened in Arkham. "Clock's not tickin' for me, sweetheart. I am the clock. C'mon, Mags. You got one move left before this whole room resets and I have to go back to bein' bored."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie raises her hands. "We could all eat in peace if nobody plays hero today. What do you say?"
turns.presentation_text: Under the mess hall's hard light, Harley plucked the spoon from between her teeth, flipped it once across her knuckles, and spun on her heel toward the scrape of the plastic chair at the far end, chin up and both hands out as if bringing up a house light on the new stander. 'Ooooh! Did somebody just stand up for a better seat? 'Cause that's what I like to hear — an audience that knows the price of admission. Get comfy, sweetheart, the show ain't got a refund policy.' She turned back and walked the lane slowly — past Ivy's table, past the dragged-out empty tray, past the stalled patch of floor where Magpie's drift had stopped — then planted herself square between the new girl and the table, back to the trustee, back to the far door, eyes still catching the gold flash at the guard's wrist. 'And you, Sparkly. Peace? You're standin' in the middle of my carnival askin' for quiet? Nah, pumpkin. Quiet's what they do to you after lights-out. You wanna make nice, you picked the wrong lane.' 'So here's how it goes — you want the shine, you take the shine, and I'll be right here narratin' it for the cheap seats. You want the table and the salad and the little voice tellin' you to behave? Then say it out loud so Ivie can hear her lettuce dyin' in your mouth. Either way, I'm the one you dance with first. Clock didn't stop, sugar. It just got a better drummer.' She popped the spoon back between her teeth like a rose stem, rocked back on her heels, and pointed one finger at the guard's wrist, then at Magpie's stalled stretch of floor, then at her own chest — an invitation tapped out in three little beats while the room watched and the chair scrape at the far end marked new weight shifting for a better view.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie leans back. "Nobody's walking out of here clean. Stop pretending otherwise."
turns.presentation_text: Poison Ivy stayed seated on the bench, spine straight, both palms flat on either side of her tray, and did not rise to meet the stance Harley had planted between Magpie and the table. When the overhead fluorescent stuttered a half-beat and the room's low hum dropped out entirely for one second, she let that silence sit untouched — no movement, no sound — watching the flat of Harley's shoulders and the empty lane behind her, where the trustee beside the tray return had stopped moving. Only when the hum came back did she hook the dragged-out second tray with two fingers and ease it a half-inch closer to the seat beside her, an unhurried correction of the table's arrangement. Her hand lifted from the tray and came to rest on the table's edge, index finger laid along the corner, the nail pale under the flicker. Her eyes traveled the open lane in front of her — past Harley's planted stance and the spoon between her teeth, past the stalled patch of floor where Magpie's drift had ended, to the gold flash at the guard's wrist and the far door beyond it — then settled back on Harley with the patience of someone reading a gauge that had already stopped moving. She said, "Harley. You've turned your back on me twice in one meal, and now you've turned it on the door as well. That's not a carnival. That's a woman standing in a lane with her back to the exit, holding a spoon, and calling it a drum. The hum just went out of this room for a full second, and every guard on the wall heard it land on you. You wanted the lights; you have them. But the next line out of this table is still mine, and you can stand there and be my scenery for it, or you can sit and keep the teeth I like." She turned her eyes down the lane toward the girl who had stopped drifting and said, "Sparkly. Look at him. Back to the trustee, back to the far door, both hands free, narrating your future for the cheap seats—and the only thing between you and the exit is a woman in a harlequin's mood. That is the whole offer, spelled out. So here is mine, said the last time: the seat beside me is warm, the tray in front of it is not metal, and the terms have not changed. One true thing, spoken here, at this table. Do that and the lane forgets you stood in it. Don't, and when that door opens you'll be explaining your appetite to whoever walks through it, with his back still turned and my patience already spent."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie stands as guards approach. "If you're moving us, say where. I don't like surprises."
turns.presentation_text: The second guard's shoulder radio crackled with a clipped transmission, and the fluorescent hum came back up thin and high over the tables. Harley plucked the spoon out from between her teeth, rapped it twice flat against her own palm, and swiveled her head toward the sound — tracking it across the mess hall without giving up one inch of the lane she had planted in. She tipped her chin at the stuttering light like it had just bought a ticket. Harley's voice came out flat and bright across the tables: "NEXT line's yours, huh? Ivie, sweetheart, you keep sayin' that like the room's gotta wait its turn for the bathroom. Look around! Nobody's waitin'. Radio's talkin', the lights are hummin', and I'm still the only thing in this cafeteria with a heartbeat and a punchline. You want the table? Take the table! Nobody's fightin' you for a tray of wet lettuce. But the lane? The lane is MINE, baby. I built it outta nothin' but a spoon and a bored afternoon." Harley hooked a thumb at the far door behind her without turning around, then backed up the lane two slow, showy steps — arms spread wide, the spoon held out to one side like a ringmaster's baton — until her shoulder blades bumped the door frame itself. She rocked back against it, hips cocked, grin all teeth, splitting the room between Ivy's table and the watch on the guard's wrist. "Sparkly! You hear that radio? That's the sound of somebody upstairs writin' a name down. Could be yours. Could be mine — I'm not picky, I'm famous. So here's the last offer on the board, and I ain't repeatin' it, 'cause a lady's got a brand to protect. You want the shine? Then take the shine and give this whole ward a story to jack off to at lights-out. You want the salad bar and the quiet little voice tellin' you to be good? Then walk over there and say it out loud so Ivie hears her lettuce gettin' a new roommate. But either way, pumpkin — you dance through ME first. 'Cause I'm standin' on the exit, I'm holdin' the clock, and I don't do refunds."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie shuffles in the transfer line, eyes on the corridor cameras. "Mess hall's done. What's next—punishment or opportunity?"
turns.presentation_text: Ivy rose from the bench without hurry, hooked her tray with one hand, and crossed to the tray return along the table's edge rather than through the open lane, keeping the whole carnival at her back and giving Harley's doorway stance a wide, deliberate berth. The hard fluorescents buzzed thin overhead. She set the tray down flat, lifted the split lettuce leaf and the cracked grain of rice into her palm, and turned to face the room from the end of the tables, arms loose, chin level. "Keep the lane, Harley. You built it out of a spoon and a bored afternoon—I wouldn't dream of charging admission to something that small. But hear the part you keep skipping: you're standing on the exit with your back to it, and the only people in this room who get paid to watch a show are the ones on the walls. That crackle in the second guard's radio wasn't applause. It was a name. Yours, mine, or hers—they haven't finished writing it. I don't need the middle of the floor to know which way that door opens. You do." At the tray return, beside the spilled tray near the service door, she lowered one knee toward the floor and turned a broken shard of ceramic over with two fingers, reading the wet mash smeared beneath it. She pressed her thumb into the spill, and a single pale filament slipped out of the split vein in the lettuce leaf across her palm, wicked down into the mash, and disappeared — no flourish, no reach, nothing a guard on the wall would bother to log. She closed her hand over the leaf and stilled it. "Sparkly. You've heard two offers and neither one is a third. So here is not an offer—here is a question, and it's the last one this room will ask you today. Not what the shine is. Not what the lane is. What you came through that door for. Answer it and I'll know whether you're a cutting worth keeping alive or compost that wandered in front of the wrong window. Don't answer, and I'll assume the second, and so will every guard in here, and you'll spend the rest of your stay explaining your appetite to people who don't ask questions at all." Ivy straightened, left the broken shard where it lay, and stayed standing at the tray return — not returning to the bench, not stepping into the lane, not looking at Harley at all. Her eyes tracked the open floor between the tables and the far door beyond it, unhurried, settled, waiting on the only answer that was ever hers to take.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie forces a laugh. "We're all victims here, right? Maybe we stop biting each other."
turns.presentation_text: Harley rolled her shoulder blades off the door frame, flipped the spoon once flat across her knuckles, and came back down the lane slow — not hurrying, hips leading, chin up, eyes on Ivy's turned back at the tray return the whole way, through the hard light and the scrape of chairs she refused to turn toward. The fluorescent hum rode high and thin over the long tables; at the room's margin the guards stayed where they were, one wrist flashing gold under the tubes. "Well look at that. Ivie WALKS. Walks away from the table, walks away from the lane, walks all the way down to the garbage like the garbage got better jokes. Sweetheart, you don't get to close the show after I bought the fireworks. And you — you don't get to stand there readin' the floor like it's gonna answer for you." She planted one boot heel on the rim of the spilled tray by the service door, tipped it once with her toe, and rapped the spoon twice flat against the tray return's edge — sliding herself into the gap between Ivy and the far door so the room had to look through Harley to see either one of them. Cold air off the service door crawled along the tile and carried up the smell of mop water. "Sparkly! New girl! You hear that? Question's been asked twice now and you're still standin' there like a coat rack with a heartbeat. Ivy wants to know what you came through that door for. Fine. So do I. But here's the difference, pumpkin — she asked you nice, and I'm askin' you loud. So say it to my face, or let the nice men on the wall write it down for you. Either way it comes outta your mouth before that hum drops again. Clock's still mine. I'm callin' the last dance." She flipped the spoon up, caught it, and tapped out the same three beats — Magpie's stalled patch of floor, the gold flash at the guard's wrist, her own chest — faster this time, twice each, like a countdown. Then she rocked back on her heels, grin all teeth, and stayed planted between the tray return and the lane, waiting for the room to give her the answer it owed her.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie looks at Ivy, not Harley. "I kept your secret. That means something, even in here."
turns.presentation_text: Ivy did not step back from the tray return as Harley's spoon rapped its edge. She laid her closed hand flat on the rim, over the split lettuce leaf she still held, and let the sound die without answering it—chin level, her eyes traveling from Harley's planted stance and the spoon to the stalled stretch of floor past her, then back, unhurried, as if reading a gauge that had not moved. The fluorescent hum stayed flat and even over the long tables. "Harley. You've backed your whole carnival up against the serving hatch, which means you're finally standing somewhere the room can smell you. There's nothing behind you but the door and a guard who's already decided what your name is worth. Keep tapping. It's a nice sound.
