Which means the clock in this room ain't mine an' it ain't Red's. It's his. An' he don't drum." Harley leaned in over the chair's spine, sliding her open palm one slow inch further across the plastic toward Magpie's end of the table — still her own movement, still empty, still not touching anything — and stopped with her fingertips a hand's width from the edge where Magpie's hands would be. She kept her chin down, eyes up, grin going wide and slow, and did not blink away. She said, "Tick. Birdie. That's the loud one, an' it's the last one I'm gonna give ya for free. Red's word holds an' mine's got teeth, an' the pen is three steps from your name. You say somethin' to this room, right now, an' you're a person at a table. You don't, an' you're just a fist an' a wristband an' a whole lotta nothin' — an' then I get to find out what Red actually does when the hands come off her thighs. I already know. She plants. Question is what you do. So go on. Open your mouth, sweetpea. I'm right here."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie nods at the scratched key tag. "East stairwell. That's where trouble lives."
turns.presentation_text:
A metal tray clattered off the serving-line rail at the far end of the room, and every conversation dropped a register for a beat. Ivy did not turn her head toward it. She let the sound pass through the room the way she let everything pass — as a fact, not a cue — and stayed planted on Magpie's other side, weight even on both feet, both hands open and visible at her thighs with the thumbs turned out where the wall could count them. Then she lifted her right hand off her thigh and laid it flat on the empty length of scarred plastic in the strip between Harley's outstretched palm and the end of the table, half a hand's width from Harley's fingers and not touching, and drew it back an inch, leaving the print of her fingers on the plastic.

"Every head at this table just checked the rail, Harls. None of them checked you. That's what you keep missing. You don't hold a room's clock by drumming on it — you hold it by being the only thing in it that doesn't flinch when something falls. You've been loud for five turns and the room still looks up when a tray hits the floor. Sit in your chair, keep your hand where it is, and let the quiet do the part you keep trying to shout over."

She did not look at Harley after she said it. Her gaze traveled the familiar line — Harley's open palm on the plastic, the empty strip she had just printed with her fingers, across the aisle to the guard level with the middle of the long table, clipboard in hand, gold watch loose on the wrist — and settled on the end of the table where Magpie's silence had been sitting. Her chin stayed level, her breathing stayed even, and she did not blink away.

"Margaret. I told this room I would step back, and I'm correcting myself, because stepping back is the lazy version of what I actually want. So here it is shortened. One word, out loud, to this table. Not to me, not to her, not to the man with the clipboard — to the room. And you should know what that one word buys before you spend it or swallow it. It buys the quiet continuing past lunch. Whatever you're carrying, it moves quiet through me, exactly the way my word said it would — nothing in your hand walks out of this room through me, and I don't hand you to the loud one for it. That's a promise with roots on it. You've had it since the trays came out and you haven't spent it once. This is the last turn I hold it open. Say a word, or I stop being the door and start being the wall — and you'll find out which one this room prefers. I don't repeat myself for appetite, Margaret. I'm not repeating myself now."

Ivy stayed exactly where her last step had left her — across from Harley, closer to the guard's sightline, both hands open and visible, the print of her fingers still on the strip of plastic between them. She did not reach for Harley's hand and did not reach for Magpie. She left the mark where it sat and held her eyes on the end of the table without blinking away.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie doesn't soften her voice. "If you sell me out, I'll make sure you regret it before lights-out."
turns.presentation_text: Under the hard fluorescents of the mess hall, the long tables sat in parallel rows and the guard wall kept its clipboard level with the middle of the room. Harley stayed dropped onto the backwards chair, knees hooked wide around the seat back, and slid her open left palm flat across the scarred plastic until it lay just beside the fresh print Ivy had left — half a hand's width away, not touching, fingers loose and countable for the wall. She hooked her chin back over her shoulder and let her eyes make the short trip up the aisle to the guard level with the middle of the long table: clipboard, pen, gold watch, all of it still writing. Then she rolled her gaze back down the table. "Awww. Look at that. Red's got a new mark on the board. One for me, one for you, one for the man with the pen. You collectin' fingerprints or roommates, sugar? 'Cause I already got a chair, a nickname, an' a whole personality. You're gonna need a bigger table." She rocked the chair back till it balanced on two legs, both hands still open on the plastic, and kept her eyes pinned down the table without blinking away. "Birdie. Hey. Birdie. You still in there? 'Cause my girl just did a full lap around this table to park herself on your other side with both hands where the wall can count 'em — an' you didn't twitch at that either. So here's where I'm at. I don't want the watch. Never did. I don't want whatever's breathin' in your fist. I want one word. One. Said out loud, to me, where the whole cafeteria gets to watch it come outta your mouth. Not to Red. Not to the pen. Not to the air over the table. To me." "An' before you decide the price is too high — look at the man with the clipboard. Pen's still up. Line's still empty. He's waitin' on the same word I am. That's the only clock in this room worth watchin', an' it's tickin' at my table now. So go on. Open your mouth, sweetpea. I'm right here. I ain't goin' anywhere."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie lets the guards hurry her along. "This isn't over. It's just moving rooms."
turns.presentation_text:
Magpie let the guards hurry her along, and the far mess-hall door's bar-lock clanked home twice as the escort pushed her through.

Ivy did not turn her head toward it. The double clank landed in the room the way she let everything land — as a fact, not a cue — and she kept her feet where her last step had left them, weight even, both hands open and visible.

Her gaze took the well-worn line one final time: the empty end of the table, the strip of scarred plastic still holding the print of her fingers, the guard level with the middle of the long table, the clipboard in his hand, the pen still not landed on the paper.

The heat lamp's orange glare swung across the plastic between the two women, and she watched it cross her own print without moving to cover it.

“There's your word, Harls. It came from the door, not the table. Twice. You spent six turns and a chair and a nickname trying to get one syllable out of her, and the room answered with a bar-lock instead — which means the pen never had to ask, and neither did you. That's the whole verdict on appetite. It doesn't leave a person behind when it walks out. It just leaves a fist.”

Ivy lifted her right hand off the strip of plastic — leaving the print where it sat, uncovered, in the open light — and set it back at her thigh, thumb turned out, fingers loose, both hands countable for the wall. She took one measured step back from the contested length of table, out of the glare's swinging line, and came to rest beside her own tray. She did not touch it, and she did not look at the vacated end of the bench. Her chin stayed level, her breathing even, and her eyes came to rest on Harley and stayed there for the first time in six turns.

“Now hear the rest of it while the room is still quiet, because I only say it once. My word held. I said nothing in her fist would walk out through me, and nothing did — that offer is spent, not broken, and I'm not spending a second one on a coat rack that never learned to speak. So the clock stops here. You can keep the chair, the bench, the nickname, the hand on the plastic — all of it was mine to lend and none of it was ever yours to count with. What you don't keep is the room. You've been loud for six turns, and the only thing in this cafeteria that ticked was a door you never opened. Put your hand back on your side of the table, Harls. The quiet's mine now, and I intend to spend it on something that grows.”

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie keeps her eyes on the guard's gold watch while she pushes food around her tray. "Pretty things never stay pretty in here for long."
turns.presentation_text:
Harley hooked a plastic chair with her ankle and dragged it out sideways, then planted both heels up on the table edge hard enough to rattle the tray. The mess hall's hard lighting stripped the worn murals to bare color and kept every table in view of the guards at the margin.

"Oooooh, lookit the room go quiet! Everybody feel that? That's the sound a bad idea makes when it's still wearin' its church clothes."

She rolled her shoulders and tipped her head toward the guard line, tracking the little gold flash she'd caught there before cutting her eyes back across the tables. A tray corner scraped the long table as a chair dragged back two seats down; a guard's radio crackled once at the room's margin, drawing a few eyes toward the sound before they slid back to the tables.

"Hey. New girl. Magpie, right? Ya got that look like somebody just dangled a present in front'a ya and told ya not to touch."

She slid her elbows onto the table and propped her chin in both hands, grin wide and all teeth, leaning into the space between them like she was about to share a secret instead of start a fire.

"So what was it, huh? What'd ya see? C'mon, tell Auntie Harley. I promise I'll only laugh a normal amount."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie murmurs to Ivy, "Whatever happened to that nurse who kept staring at our table last month?"
turns.presentation_text: Ivy didn't shift for Harley's chair-theatrics. She set her plastic fork down at a precise angle, tines aligned with the tray's edge, and folded her hands over the table like she was filing the room away. Her gaze tracked once along the guard line, settling briefly where the gold flashed, then returned across the table. Under the mess hall's hard lighting, the worn murals and long tables kept everything public, and the tray clatter pressed in from all sides. "You saw the watch. That's not the interesting part — half the ward saw the watch. The interesting part is that you looked at it the way a plant looks at a crack in the pavement." "So let's be precise, new girl. Harley's the one who'll laugh. I'm the one who decides whether the idea you're chewing on gets to grow. Which is it — are you useful, or are you a mess I'll have to keep sweeping off this table?" She leaned back an inch, elbows still on the table, and let her voice drop below the tray clatter — quiet enough that only the three of them could hear it, sharp enough that it cut the way Harley's grin didn't.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie flicks a glance at Harley. "You want a distraction. She wants a favor. I'm listening to both of you."
turns.presentation_text: Harley barked out a laugh that cut across the tray clatter, then let her heels drop off the table edge and slap the floor. She rolled her neck once, slow and showy, keeping both hands flat on the table like she was pinning the whole ward down in place, while the hard lights laid every scratched tray and worn mural edge in plain view. “Whoa, whoa, whoa — holds the phone, Red. Ya don't get to do the scary part. I called dibs on the new girl's first flinch, that's like a sacred Arkham tradition, I got a punch card an' everythin'.” She swung her attention back across the table, chin tilting up, grin going lopsided and mean around the edges. One thumb tapped twice against the tabletop, a little drumroll nobody asked for, and her eyes cut sideways along the guard line — catching the gold glint again before snapping back. At the far door, a second guard drifted into the aisle and began angling closer to their table. “An' you. Yeah, you. Don't go hide behind Ivy's vocabulary, she does that on purpose, it's a trap. I asked you a real question an' the clock's tickin'. That little gold flash up the guard line? Half the room saw it, sure, but you're the one who saw it an' went quiet. Quiet's my least favorite sound. So spill, pigeon — was it the shine, or was it the wrist wearin' it? 'Cause those are two very different kinda bad ideas an' I only got one afternoon.” Harley propped one elbow on the table and hooked her thumb toward the aisle without looking away from Magpie, still grinning, still leaning in like the answer was a secret she was already halfway to stealing.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie notes the scratched tag on the guard's key ring without staring. "East stairwell must be popular."
turns.presentation_text: Ivy let Harley's laugh break and spend itself against the clatter of trays before she answered it. She reached down and turned her plastic fork a quarter-turn out of the line she'd set it in, the only motion her hands made, then laid her palm flat against the table edge as if taking the table's temperature. "You called dibs. I heard you, and I'll even let you keep it. But look at the shape of what you just asked her — shine, or the wrist wearing it. That's a question with a right answer, Harley. You don't ask questions that have right answers unless you've already decided you want the answer. Which means you're not playing anymore, you're shopping." Her eyes traveled once down the aisle without turning her head, past the wall line, to where the second guard had drifted in and stopped with his thumbs hooked in his belt, close enough now that a dropped fork would be a decision. Ivy registered him and gave nothing back, gaze returning across the table with the same flat patience. "So here's the part you keep skipping, pigeon. Whoever's wearing that watch walks this room for another six hours. Whatever you're chewing on, you're chewing it in front of a man who can hear you swallow. That's not me being dramatic, that's just the architecture. So answer Harley, or answer me — I genuinely don't care which — but pick a lane before the lane picks you. I've watched things grow in worse ground than this table. I've also watched them get pulled up by the roots for being slow." She sat back and folded her hands over the tray again, tines realigned to nothing in particular, chin level, expression unhurried, leaving the space across the table open and the pressure sitting in it.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie whispers, "If I help you move that packet, you don't sell me to Harley when it goes wrong."
turns.presentation_text: The mess hall's hard lights flattened everything to the same white glare, and the tray clatter hadn't thinned. Ivy lifted the plastic fork off her tray between two fingers and turned it upright, tines up, holding it level between the three of them like a specimen she'd already decided not to keep. "Keep your dibs, Harley. I'll even let you keep the punch card. But look at the aisle instead of the pigeon — he stopped. He isn't walking, he's waiting. That means the room already has a clock on it, and it isn't yours." She lowered the fork and set it down pointing across the room, tines toward the wall line, then slid her tray an inch away from her until her half of the table was bare plastic. "So. Whatever question you're holding, hold it six hours. Not out of kindness — because anything said at this table today gets repeated by a man with a radio before the trays are cleared. That's not a warning, that's the architecture. You want a lane, there's exactly one: grow something small and quiet and useful, or get pulled up by the roots. I don't bend the rule for new growth and I don't bend it for you." She picked the limp shred of green off the tray's lip, folded it once between thumb and forefinger—small, neat, unhurried—and tucked it under the table rim where the guard's sightline didn't reach. A cutting, not a threat. "Laundry's on the north run after count. If what you saw is worth more than the watch, it can keep that long. If it can't — then it isn't an idea, it's a symptom, and I don't keep symptoms at my table. Harley will laugh either way. I'm the one who decides which one you are."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie smiles without warmth. "What would you trade for a guard looking the wrong way for ten seconds?"
turns.presentation_text: Harley brought both palms down flat on the tabletop, hard enough that the tray jumped and the cutlery rang against the plastic. Before the sound died she hooked her chair with one ankle and hauled it half a foot around the corner of the table, boot heel scraping all the way, until she sat angled into the aisle side with the hard overhead light flat across her face. "Six hours. Six hours! Red, listen to yaself — ya just handed the new girl a bedtime an' called it a philosophy. Nobody ever got anywhere in this dump by sittin' on a secret till laundry. That's not a rule, that's a nap." She leaned over and flicked the upright fork flat with one knuckle, sending it spinning toward the tray's lip with its tines pointing at nothing at all. Then she planted her boot up on the bench beside her and settled both forearms on her knee, chin jutted across the table at Magpie. "An' you. Ten seconds on a guard, huh? That's a real cute little number, pigeon. Cute like a firecracker's cute. Ten seconds is how long it takes to get caught, not how long it takes to get clear — an' lookit the aisle, he stopped walkin'. He's just standin' there with his thumbs in his belt like a lawn ornament, so your ten seconds already got spent before ya offered it." Two fingers drummed twice on the scarred laminate, and her grin went crooked as she stayed leaned in with her eyes locked across the table, not blinking when a chair leg squeaked two tables over and somebody shifted to watch. "So here's your lane, since everybody's so into lanes today. Red wants a cutting — small, quiet, useful. I want a scream. Somewhere in between there's you pickin' one out loud before the trays get cleared, 'cause I ain't doin' a six-hour wait for a girl who can't even say what kinda bad idea she is. Shine, wrist, or the ten seconds. Say it, pigeon. Auntie Harley's clock is the only one in this room that don't reset." Under the hard lights the long tables stayed parallel and the guard at the margin kept his thumbs hooked in his belt.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie palms the mess hall token under the tray. "Little things buy bigger mistakes in Arkham."
turns.presentation_text: Harley's palm-slap was still ringing in the tray when Ivy waited it out, letting the echo drain away before she moved at all. Then she reached across and took the flattened fork by the handle, set it back down along the tray's edge with the tines turned quietly inward — not repaired into a pointer, just returned to being cutlery. There it is. The clock that doesn't reset, wasted on a clock that already stopped. You wanted a scream, Harley. You got a room watching you want one. That's not the same thing. She doesn't look at Harley when she says it. Her eyes stay level across the table, on the space Harley just leaned into — the open half of the table, the aisle side, the distance between what was asked and what's actually on offer. So. Two questions on this table, pigeon, and only one of them has a short answer. Harley's is a party trick — shine, wrist, ten seconds, pick a costume. Mine is smaller. You don't owe either of us a category. You owe the table one true thing. When the gold moved, what were you doing with your eyes — measuring the exit, or measuring the man? That's all. Say that, and the rest of it can keep until the north run. Ivy slid her tray the inch back into its place and laid her forearm flat along the table's edge, elbow tucked, hand open, taking her half of the table back without hurry. Her gaze flicked once down the aisle — the guard was still standing with his thumbs hooked in his belt, still not walking — and then came back, unhurried, to hold the space across the table. At the room's margin the radio clicked over to a new channel, and the aisle guard shifted his weight, boot sole grinding once against the floor.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie kicks a ceramic shard aside. "Someone's going to blame us for this mess unless we move."
turns.presentation_text: Harley dropped her boot off the bench and came half up out of the chair, both palms still pinned to the tabletop, dragging the seat corner with her so the plastic leg screeched across the floor and the aisle-side half of the table belonged to her. She cut her eyes once up the guard line — same thumbs-in-the-belt standstill, same gold sitting on his wrist doing nothing — and held there a beat too long before snapping back. "Exit or the man. Exit or the man. Red, that's not a question, that's a survey — you handin' out clipboards now? Here, I'll save ya the tally: I measure the wrist. Not the shine, not the aisle, the wrist, 'cause the wrist is attached to a fella who stopped walkin' 'cause he heard his own name in his head. That's my true thing, pigeon, there's your answer, free of charge. Ivy got the small one an' I got the loud one an' you got both of 'em starin' at ya, so pick." She snatched the fork Ivy had set down, snapped it once across her knee — the plastic popping loud enough that two rows back went quiet and heads turned into the aisle — and dropped the halves on the tray like a tip. She hooked her thumb at the wall line without looking at it, grin going crooked, chin still jutted across the table. At the margin, the guard shifted his stance and lifted the radio to his mouth without keying it. "Ten seconds, huh? Cute. Ten seconds is a girl askin' permission with her eyes. I don't do ten — I do however long it takes the room to decide it didn't see nothin'. But hey, you wanna move, sweetheart, then move. Right now. In front of the lawn ornament, in front of the walls, in front of Red an' her cuttin' box an' her six-hour bedtime. Don't tell me about the ten seconds, show me the first one, 'cause Auntie Harley's clock just ran out an' I'm real curious what you do when nobody hands you a lane."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie raises her hands. "We could all eat in peace if nobody plays hero today. What do you say?"
turns.presentation_text:
Ivy didn't reach for the fork. She let the two snapped halves lie where Harley had dropped them on the tray, then slid the tray — plate, plastic, and broken cutlery together — the rest of the way across the line Harley had dragged with her chair, until it sat entirely on Harley's side of the table. She didn't take it back. She laid both forearms on the bare plastic in front of her, hands open, and left the ceded half exactly where it was.

Her eyes traveled once down the aisle — the guard still standing with his thumbs hooked in his belt, gold still sitting on his wrist, still doing nothing with it — then on to the far door, where a second man had stepped in and stopped with one hand on the frame, watching the aisle guard instead of the tables. She gave him nothing back, looked away first, and returned to the space across the table without any hurry in it at all.

"There it is. You broke cutlery in front of two men paid to count your hands, and you did it to hand a stranger a deadline. That isn't a scream, Harley. It's a receipt, and the room already filed it."

"You wanted the table — take it, you've got it, tray and all. You wanted a scream. You'll get one, and it won't be hers, and it won't be the one you're fishing for. The aisle has a door in it now, and you spent the whole afternoon's noise on a piece of plastic. So sit down, or keep standing and be the exhibit. Either way, my half of this was decided before you hooked that chair."

"Pigeon. Six hours was a lane. She just burned it, so here's what's left: nothing else gets said at this table for the rest of the meal. Not out of kindness — because a room that remembers a fork is a room that forgets a name, and I'd rather it forget a name. What you saw, you hold. North run, after count, if it's worth more than a watch. If it isn't, don't come, and I'll know which one you were without anyone raising their voice about it."

Under the table rim, where the guard's sightline didn't reach, she found the folded shred of green she had left there and nudged it deeper into the seam with one thumb — small, neat, unhurried. Still a cutting, still hers, still quiet. Then she folded her hands on the bare half of the table and settled back, watching the aisle instead of the pigeon.

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie leans back. "Nobody's walking out of here clean. Stop pretending otherwise."
turns.presentation_text: Under the hard mess-hall lighting, trays and plastic chairs sat in parallel rows and the ward watched in its usual low-privacy sprawl. Harley's head snapped toward the tray-return window the instant the trustee dumped the stack into the bin, a hard clatter that pulled the aisle guard's chin around for one full second — she was already looking before he was. She swung back with her grin wide and mean, catching the exact moment his thumbs went still in his belt, and slapped the tabletop once, flat, hooking a thumb at the empty half Ivy had ceded her. "See that? One second. One whole second where the lawn ornament's countin' trays instead of us. Thanks, sweetheart, whoever you are — Auntie Harley's buyin'. Red, nice slide. Real tidy. You gave away half a table to prove a point an' I'm gonna spend it. She rolls her neck until it pops, then drops both elbows onto the bare plastic Ivy cleared, claiming it the way an animal claims a sunbeam." She hooked the spare plastic chair with her heel and dragged it screeching into the aisle-side gap, planted sideways so she straddled the space between the table and the walkway, one boot up on the seat, forearms on her knee. She cut her eyes down the aisle once — the guard was already turning back — and held the look until she had the timing, then let it snap back across the table. "An' pigeon. You heard me the first time an' ya stood there with your ten seconds hangin' out like a tongue, so here's the update. Window's closin'. They got forks on this table — one's in two pieces an' one's just plastic an' both of 'em are already a receipt, so don't go lookin' at me for a prop. You said ten seconds, I said show me the first one. So show me. Right now, in front of the door an' the frame an' the second fella pretendin' he ain't watchin'. Or don't — but if ya don't, then ya sat there an' let Red hand you a bedtime an' let me hand you a clock, an' the whole room gets to decide what that makes ya. C'mon, pigeon. Auntie's got one second left an' she's spendin' it on you."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie stands as guards approach. "If you're moving us, say where. I don't like surprises."
turns.presentation_text: The far door swung shut and the flat crack of it rolled across the tables, and the second guard stepped fully inside the frame. Still Poison Ivy's hands stayed open and flat on the bare plastic. She did not turn her head — only let her gaze travel once down the aisle to him, then back to the table, unhurried, her thumb pressing the folded shred of green a fraction deeper into the seam beneath the rim. "That's a door, Harley. Not a scream, not a count, not a clock you own — steel on steel, and a second man inside it. You spent the whole afternoon teaching this room your timing, and the room just answered you with a lock. Sit down. Not for her, not for me. For the arithmetic." She lifted both palms an inch off the table, turned them over slowly, and laid them back down empty — deliberate enough that the guard line caught the gesture and nothing else — then drew her forearms in until she occupied only her own half of the plastic. "Pigeon. You asked the aisle to answer you, and it answered. So here's the small true thing, and it doesn't care whether you're sitting or standing when you say it back: nothing moves at this table while that door is still settling. North run, after count — that's where a thing that's worth more than a watch gets to grow, and where a thing that isn't gets buried without anyone raising their voice about it." "So look at the room instead of the man in it. Harley got her scream — it's the quiet kind, and she hates it. What's left is whether you're still an idea. I've decided nothing yet. That should worry you more than the watch did, if you're smart, and relieve you, if you're useful."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie shuffles in the transfer line, eyes on the corridor cameras. "Mess hall's done. What's next—punishment or opportunity?"
turns.presentation_text: A short burst of static from the aisle guard's radio cracked across the mess hall, cutting over the long tables and worn murals under the hard lights. Harley Quinn snapped toward it — chin up, shoulders squaring, boot scraping off the seat as she came up half a step into the aisle gap she had already been straddling. She clocked the guard's hand on the radio, then the second man still inside the door frame, then swung back around the corner of the table with her grin already loaded and mean. “Ooooh, didja hear that? Little walkie-talkie went chirp! That’s Arkham’s version of a doorbell, pigeon — means somebody up front just got told a story about this table. Now they’re all standin’ around lookin’ important with their thumbs in their belts an’ their thumbs in their radios, an’ Red here’s gonna tell ya it’s a lock. It ain’t a lock. It’s a countdown with a lisp.” She hooked the plastic chair behind her with one heel and dragged it a few inches further into the aisle — not out of the way, into it — then planted her boot back up on the seat and dropped both forearms across her knee, chin aimed across the table like the whole ward was just a set she was waiting on. “An’ you, Red. Sit down for the arithmetic, sit down for the a-rith-me-tic, six hours, north run, grow somethin’ small — ya know what that sounds like? It sounds like a girl who already picked which door she’s leavin’ through an’ don’t wanna show the class her permission slip. That’s fine. That’s real fine. I ain’t mad at ya. I’m just sayin’ the lawn ornament’s got a radio now an’ my clock’s got a second hand an’ the second hand’s the only one in this room that tells the truth.” “So here’s the new dare, pigeon, since ol’ Harley’s generous — ’cause I am, I’m a giver, ask anybody. I ain’t askin’ whether ya bite. I’m askin’ what shape the bite is. Do ya stand up, or do ya go quiet like Red wants? Do ya look at the wrist or the aisle? Do ya do it now, or do ya do it after the door stops swingin’? See, all of those are movin’, an’ only one of ’em’s a lie, an’ I already know which one — ’cause the room’s still lookin’ at you, sweetheart, an’ the room don’t ever look at a girl who’s about to sit still. Auntie Harley’s got her hand on the clock. Don’t make me turn it over.”

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie forces a laugh. "We're all victims here, right? Maybe we stop biting each other."
turns.presentation_text:
Ivy didn't rise when Harley hauled the chair further into the aisle. Both her palms stayed flat on her half of the bare plastic; she turned her head only far enough to catch the guard's hand sliding off the radio down to his belt, and the second man still standing inside the door frame, before her gaze came back across the table, unhurried. The chair in the walkway she didn't look at — she looked past it, the way you look past furniture you've already decided to outlive. At the room's margin the radio crackled back, a voice too low to parse, and the guard clipped it to his belt without answering.

"He didn't answer it. That's the part you heard wrong, Harley. A radio that chirps and gets clipped back to a belt isn't a doorbell — it's a man being told to stop being interesting, and complying. So no, it isn't a countdown, and it isn't a lock either. It's the room deciding this table is already filed. You spent the afternoon building a clock. They've stopped reading the time."

Under the table rim, out of the guard line's sight, her thumb found the folded shred of green she'd left in the seam and pressed it a fraction deeper — small, neat, the only motion in her hands. Then she laid one hand open on the table between the three of them, palm up, fingers straight, leaving it there like a scale waiting for something to be weighed on it.

"And you, pigeon. He keeps asking what shape the bite is, because he wants to watch you pick a costume. I don't. I want one number, and then we're done until the north run. When that watch flashed and the room went quiet, what did you leave with — the thing you could take, or the man you could use? Because one of those is worth carrying past count, and the other is a fork snapped over somebody's knee. So say the number. Not the shine, not the aisle. What is it worth, and is it worth more than the wrist it sits on? That's the only true thing on this table, and I've already told you which table you're sitting at."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie looks at Ivy, not Harley. "I kept your secret. That means something, even in here."
turns.presentation_text: Harley's head ticked sideways first — not toward the table, but toward the wall, where the second man had peeled off the paint and started the long slow walk toward the aisle gap, hands loose at his sides, walking the way men walk when they've already decided you're the story they'll tell later. She watched him two full steps, lips peeling back off her teeth, then swung her chin back around the corner of the table as if she'd just found a better toy in the room. "Oooooooh. Look at that, look at that — wall guy's walkin'. He's doin' the slow one. The slow one's my favorite, that's the one where they practice it in the mirror an' still get it wrong." She planted both palms on the sideways chair and rocked it once onto its back legs, tipping herself further into the aisle gap while her boot sole scraped a long note out of the tile. She wasn't clearing the walkway — she was making it hers, spreading into the space the man was walking toward like a cat on a warm grate. Her eyes cut once to the guard's wrist, the gold still sitting there doing nothing, then snapped back across the table. "He ain't comin' for the pigeon, Red. He ain't comin' for the fork neither — he's comin' for you, 'cause you're the one sittin' still an' lookin' at him like a plant in a pot. Quiet attracts the lawn ornaments. That's a real thing, ask anybody, that's science, that's you." She let the chair drop back down with a plastic crack and leaned both forearms across her knee, chin jutted, grin going crooked and mean around the edges. Her thumb tapped twice on the chair back — a drumroll nobody had asked for — and her weight settled into the aisle side of the table like she'd just bought the square of floor under it. "So here's the thing, pigeon, an' I'm only gonna say it with the slow guy in earshot 'cause that's the funnest way to say a thing. Red wants a number. I want a scream. You been sittin' there holdin' both like a kid with two popsicles an' no tongue. He's got maybe six more steps before he's standin' over this table lookin' important, an' then the question answers itself whether ya like it or not. So pick one. Say the number. Or do somethin' the room can watch. Either way, sweetheart — Auntie Harley's countin' his steps now, an' I ain't startin' over when he gets here."

turns.player_stimulus: When a guard snaps at Ivy, Magpie says nothing—but her jaw tightens. Ivy notices.
turns.presentation_text: The footsteps were still coming down the aisle, unhurried, and the mess hall's hard overheads left nowhere for the sound to hide. Ivy didn't turn her head for them. She kept her eyes on Harley's boot where it pinned the sideways chair, and laid her palm flat over the seam beneath the table rim—heel down, fingers loose—so the folded green sat covered without her ever glancing at it. Across the table, Magpie's jaw had gone tight at the guard's snap, and Ivy had seen it. "You counted him out loud, Harley. Every step. You do the room's arithmetic for it and then act wounded when it answers back. Six steps of your voice and one of his boots, and you're still calling it a clock. It isn't. It's a funnel. Everything this table said today is already pouring toward the aisle, and the only question left is what's still sitting on it when he arrives." She turned her gaze across the table, past the tray, to the woman with the tightened jaw. "Pigeon. Look at me, not at him — you've had your eyes on the wrist all afternoon and it hasn't bought you a thing. When that man stops at this table, the meal ends and the door starts. So here's the whole of it, and it's the last thing I say until the north run. You don't owe Harley a costume. You don't owe me a confession. What you saw is the only object at this table that's still yours, and its price is silence — past count, past the corridor, past a green door and a shelf of dead plants, and then we see what it grows into. Say nothing now and it stays an idea. Say anything now and I file it with the fork." She lifted the palm off the seam, turned it over once, and set it back on her own knee; the green stayed where it was, still under the tray's shadow and the table's rusted edge. Her voice didn't rise, and she didn't look down the aisle again. "Harley. You wanted the scream. It's walking. You bought it, you paid for it in plastic, and it's still four steps out — so enjoy the sound, because it's the last thing this table gets for free today. Sit down, or stand there. Either way the room has stopped asking and started counting."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie mutters, "Harley wants a riot. You want a garden. I want to survive the corridor."
turns.presentation_text: The second guard halted two tables short of the aisle gap, close enough that his shadow slid long across the seam of the table rim where the folded green was hidden, and the mess hall's hard overheads made the whole room witness it at once. Harley caught the halt the instant the bootfalls quit. For about half a heartbeat she went still, which for Harley was an eternity; then she rocked the sideways chair forward instead of back and dropped both boots flat to the tile, throwing her own shadow across that same seam from the other side, fighting him for the square of floor he had just stopped on. "Ooooh — he stopped short. Two tables short, thumbs in the belt, shinin' his own little eclipse over my table. That's the slow walk, folks, that's the whole show — eight steps of theatre an' he chickens out at the good part. Sweetheart, you don't get to walk the runway an' then stand in the wings. Either come look important up close or go count trays with the other lawn ornament." She hooked both thumbs in the empty air where her belt would have been and mimed him — slow, exaggerated, chin high — for the tables behind her, then dropped it and slapped one palm flat on the aisle-side plastic, claiming the shadow's line. Her eyes cut once to Ivy, once to the green's hiding place under the rim, and came back loaded. "An' you, pigeon. Somebody at this table just told the room Auntie Harley wants a riot. Honey. A riot's what happens when the room stops pretendin' it ain't watchin'. Look around — they're watchin'. They been watchin' since the watch flashed. Red wants a number an' I want a scream an' the fella with the gold just handed us both a spotlight, so here's your last free one: stand up, sit still, or say the thing. Any of 'em's a move. None of 'em's a costume. Clock's right there on his wrist, sweetheart — go on an' read it."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie repeats quietly, "Pretty things don't stay pretty." She watches Harley's reaction.
turns.presentation_text: The tray skidded off the end of the wash counter and hit the tile, and every head on the near tables swung toward the sound before swinging back to Harley. Harley's head had whipped toward the wash counter the instant it fell, chin up, grin splitting wide, and she caught the broken shards skidding across the floor by the service door while the whole near half of the room turned with her. She let them come back. She didn't blink. Then she swung her chin around the corner of the table and planted both boots flat against the aisle-side plastic, leaning her weight into the square of floor the guard's shadow had left behind, claiming it while every eye in the ward was still pointed at her. "There it is! There's the sound I been waitin' for all afternoon — somebody dropped the whole tray line an' the room went 'huh?' like a dog hearin' a can opener. See that, pigeon? That's a riot, sweetheart. That's what one looks like. Not the kind Red's gonna tell ya about, not some quiet little seed in a crack in the pavement — a real one, with broken dishes an' everybody turnin' their head at once. An' you know what started it? Nothin'. That's the beautiful part. The room was already wound up 'cause somebody at this table said Auntie Harley wants a riot out loud, an' the room heard it, an' now the room's standin' around lookin' at me like I'm the one who threw it." She rocked the sideways chair once more, dragging it a hand's width deeper into the walkway so the aisle gap was hers — not clearing it, holding it — then dropped her boot off the seat and slapped the aisle-side plastic twice, flat, a drumroll nobody asked for. Her eyes cut once down the aisle: the same thumbs-in-the-belt standstill, the same gold sitting on the wrist doing nothing, two tables short like a man who bought a ticket and forgot the show. She hooked her thumb at the door, at the wash counter, at the shards, without looking at any of it, then brought the grin back across the table, loaded. She leaned both forearms across her knee, chin jutted across the table at the space the new girl had been holding all afternoon, thumb tapping twice on the chair back — ta-dum, ta-dum — and her weight settled into the aisle side like she had just bought the floor under it. "So here's your last free one, an' I'm callin' it 'cause the room just told us it's listenin'. Stand up. Sit still. Or say the thing. Those are the three — an' don't you dare gimme a fourth, I ain't got the patience for a fourth. Red wants a number, I want a scream, an' the fella with the gold is two tables short an' gettin' shorter every second he stands there pretendin' he ain't decided. Clock's right there on his wrist, sweetheart. Go on an' read it. Or stand up an' make me wrong. Either one's a move. Neither one's a costume."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie asks the guard, "Did the nurse who reported you get reassigned—or disappeared?"
turns.presentation_text: Ivy didn't stand, and she didn't turn her head for the boot-step. She turned her empty palm over on the bare plastic and slid it an inch toward the aisle — not into it — measuring the floor the man had just taken rather than yielding any of it, chin level, her eyes traveling once from his boots to the tray-return window and back to the seam beneath the table rim where the folded green sat out of sight. The aisle guard's jaw set; he didn't answer Magpie, but took one step forward into the aisle gap, and the tray-return window and the tables on either side of him came suddenly under the same sightline, the hard overhead light flattening the walkway to a single bright strip. Ivy said, "He stepped. Not at us — into the gap. Which means the aisle is his now, Harley, and the aisle is the only chair you've been sitting in all afternoon. He's put the tray window and both tables on one line of sight. That's not a countdown and it isn't a lock. That's a man choosing where he wants to be standing when the story gets told. You've been handing the pigeon a clock and a costume and a riot. Nobody at this table has offered her a price." Under the rim, her thumb found the folded shred of green and pressed it a fraction deeper into the seam — small, neat, the only motion her hands made. Then she drew both hands back onto her own half of the plastic and folded them, elbows in, taking up less of the table than either of the other two. "So here's the whole of it, and it's the last thing I say until the north run. Pigeon. You've been offered a number, a scream, a shape for the bite, and three ways to move. I'm not adding a fourth. What I've got is smaller and it doesn't need you to stand up, sit still, or pick a word this afternoon — it needs you quiet past count, and it needs you at the green door on the north run with whatever you're actually carrying. That's the test. Not shine, not wrist, not ten seconds. Whether the thing you saw is worth more than the room that watched you see it. Harley will laugh either way. I'm the one who decides which one you are, and I've decided nothing yet. That should worry you. North run, after count."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie fingers the token. "This buys a door. Question is whose door you want opened."
turns.presentation_text: The kitchen pass-through window banged down to a mail slot, and a second tray clattered onto the shelf behind it. Harley's chin snapped toward the sound before the tray quit ringing, her grin already splitting wide under the mess hall's hard lighting; she didn't look at the tray. She looked at the room looking at it, counting heads in the near half going up like a wave she'd ordered. "Two! Two noises in one afternoon an' I didn't have to throw either one! Somebody up front's feedin' the room on my behalf an' I ain't even tipped 'em yet. Haw! Red — Red, look at that. You told me the room filed this table. The room just banged a shutter an' dumped a tray to tell me it's still readin' the page." She rocked the sideways chair once, hard, dragging it another hand's width into the walkway until the aisle gap was hers outright, then planted one boot flat on the seat and leaned her weight across her knee. Her eyes cut down the line — the same thumbs hooked in the same belt, the same gold sitting on the wrist doing nothing, still two tables short — and she let the look ride a beat longer than she needed before snapping back. "An' you, Red. 'I've decided nothing yet.' Honey, that's not a verdict, that's a layaway. You had all afternoon to pick a lane an' ya picked the one where ya sit real still an' let the pigeon do the decidin' for ya. That's cute. That's real cute. That's you holdin' the door open an' callin' it architecture." Harley slapped the aisle-side plastic twice, flat — ta-dum, ta-dum — nobody asked for it. Her eyes flicked once to the seam under the rim where Ivy's thumb kept pushing that folded green deeper, then came back across the table loaded. "So here's your last free one, pigeon, an' I'm callin' it on account of the room's got a fresh tray an' a fresh mood. Stand up. Sit still. Or say the thing. That's three. There ain't a fourth, there ain't a 'north run,' there ain't a green door with a bedtime behind it — that's Red sellin' ya a nap an' callin' it a plant. The fella with the gold is two tables short with his thumbs in his belt an' his hand off the radio, which means he's already decided an' he's just pickin' the word for it. Clock's right there on his wrist, sweetheart. Go on an' read it. Or stand up an' make me wrong. Either one's a move. Neither one's a costume. Auntie's clock don't reset an' she just heard it tick twice."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie nods at the scratched key tag. "East stairwell. That's where trouble lives."
turns.presentation_text: The shutter stayed down at the kitchen pass-through and the second tray sat where it had landed, under the same hard light that flattened the worn murals and kept every table in the room inside every other table's line of sight. Ivy did not stand for either of them. She kept her forearms planted on her own half of the bare plastic, laid her palm flat over the seam beneath the table rim — heel of the hand down, fingers loose — and covered the folded green there without once looking at it. Her gaze moved once to the tray window, once down the aisle to the man still two tables short with his thumbs hooked in his belt and the gold on his wrist doing nothing at all, and then came back across the table with no hurry left out of it. She spoke without lifting her voice for anyone but the two opposite her. "Layaway. That's the word you liked, so let's price it. You've been paying this room all afternoon, Harley — one fork, one chair, one tray's worth of noise at a time — and calling the change a clock. It isn't a verdict and it isn't a layaway. It's rent. The aisle isn't yours. You've been renting it out loud, and the room just raised it twice while you were busy admiring the sound." She let that stand in the noise rather than over it, and turned her chin a fraction toward the third chair. "And you, pigeon. Here's the whole of it, once, and then I'm quiet until the north run. That seat has whatever the room decided it has. I'm not asking you to name it, and I'm not asking you to spend it here. My lane hasn't moved: nothing else at this table, nothing else in the aisle, nothing said in front of a man with gold on his wrist. Past count, past the corridor, at the green door — carrying whatever you're actually carrying. Come, or don't. I've decided nothing yet, and that's the last free thing this table gets today."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie doesn't soften her voice. "If you sell me out, I'll make sure you regret it before lights-out."
turns.presentation_text: Harley let Ivy's last word sit exactly as long as it took her to hook the sideways chair one more time — dragging it a hand's width deeper into the aisle gap until the walkway belonged to the chair, not the tiles. Hard light lay flat across the worn murals and the long tables, and the second tray's clatter was still dying off the tile behind the pass-through. She dropped her boot off the seat and planted both soles flat, her whole weight shifting forward onto the aisle-side plastic. Her eyes cut once down the line: same thumbs hooked in the belt, same gold doing nothing, still two tables short. She didn't wait for it to move. She looked at the room instead, catching the near half still turned her way after the shutter and the second tray banged, counting heads the way she counted drinks she hadn't paid for. "Rent! She said rent! Haw — Red, you just put a price tag on my whole afternoon an' called it a compliment. That's the nicest thing you said all day. Rent means I got the lease, sweetheart, an' you're the one sittin' on my half of the table with your hand pressed over a little green secret like a kid hidin' a cough drop from the teacher. I seen that thumb go down twice now. Twice. You ain't smooth, Red, you're just slow." She slapped the aisle-side plastic twice, flat — ta-dum, ta-dum — then hooked her thumb at the wall line without looking at it, and leaned both forearms across her knee so her chin came level with the space across the table. Her eyes flicked once to the seam under the rim where Ivy's palm sat, once down the aisle to the man two tables short with his hand off the radio, and came back loaded. "An' you. Pigeon. Red's sellin' ya a bedtime with a green door on it an' I'm sellin' ya the only real thing at this table, which is me, right here, right now, with the clock two tables out an' the room still lookin'. So I'm done askin' nice. Stand up, sit still, or say the thing — but if ya sit there an' let Red decide what kinda girl ya are, then ya ain't a pigeon, sweetheart, ya a plant. An' plants don't get to pick the pot. Auntie's clock just ticked a third time. Go on."

turns.player_stimulus: Magpie lets the guards hurry her along. "This isn't over. It's just moving rooms."
turns.presentation_text: The mess hall door clanked shut behind the guards and Magpie, and the room's low murmur did not restart. Under the hard lighting the long tables stayed bare and the shards by the service door kept their places. Ivy didn't stand for any of it. She kept her forearms on her own half of the bare plastic, and this time she didn't merely cover the seam beneath the rim — she laid two fingers along it, flattened the folded green until it lay flush, and slid it the last half-inch out of any sightline the aisle guard's belt-cam or the door frame could ever have owned. Then she drew her hand back and folded both hands in front of her, empty, unhurried, taking up less table than either of the other two. "There. That's the sound a rented afternoon makes when the tenant leaves. You called it a clock, Harley, and you called it a riot, and you called it a lease — you called it everything except what it was. A girl at a table with two women talking over her head until the door took her. The room didn't turn for you. It turned for the tray, then it turned for the door, and now it's turned back to its own plate. You wanted a scream. What you got was a steel hinge and an empty chair, and those are the two most honest things this table produced all afternoon." "And you can stop counting the fella with the gold. He's still two tables short with his thumbs in his belt because that's where they told him to be, and the radio in his pocket has already filed this table under 'nothing to see.' That's what the pigeon's exit bought us — not a riot, not a headline, a filing. So here's the arithmetic, since you like mine better when it sounds like yours. The table's still standing. The green's still under the rim. The six-hour lane still runs north, after count, past the corridor, to a green door and a shelf of dead plants. You don't have to like it. You do have to stop paying the room in plastic for a clock that already ran out." She didn't look at Harley when she said it. She looked down the aisle once, past the two-tables-short guard and the tray-return window and the shards still skidding their last inch by the service door, then brought her gaze back to the empty seat across the table. She lifted one hand and turned it palm up on the bare plastic between them — a scale, patient and unoccupied — and left it there, taking up the space the pigeon had held without pretending the pigeon was still in it. "So pick a chair and sit in it, or keep standing and be the exhibit. Either way, don't ask me to decide which one you are while the room is still watching you decide for yourself. I've decided nothing about the girl who just left. I've decided plenty about the woman still talking. North run, after count. If you're on it, you'll know what to bring. If you're not, I'll know what you were."
